analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover and pay for hospital emergency care without prior approval or network restrictions.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee in 1995 without a vote or a hearing, despite 11 cosponsors from both parties.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill responded to a real problem: federal law forces hospital emergency departments to examine and stabilize anyone who shows up, but many health plans then refused to pay for those visits, citing lack of prior approval or arguing the condition was not a true emergency. The bill would have required plans to cover emergency care regardless of whether the hospital was in their network and without prior authorization, to use a 'prudent layperson' standard for judging emergencies, to stop penalizing patients for using 911, and to pay quickly and fairly. It would have extended the same rules to Medicare and Medicaid managed care plans and set fines for violations.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in health plans, including Medicare and Medicaid managed care enrollees, who could go to any emergency department without worrying about network rules or advance approval. Emergency physicians and hospital emergency departments also benefited, because they are federally required to treat everyone and would get paid for care plans currently deny.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured people who need emergency care

how_it_helps.text: Health plans must cover emergency services whether or not the provider has a contract with the plan, and without prior authorization.
Plans must pay promptly and in a reasonable amount, and cannot impose higher cost-sharing on emergency department visits than on comparable care in other settings.
An 'emergency medical condition' is defined by what a prudent layperson with average health knowledge would reasonably believe, so coverage no longer depends on the final diagnosis.
Plans cannot discourage appropriate use of 911 or deny coverage solely because an enrollee called 911.

The same requirements apply to Medicare and Medicaid managed care plans, and states may keep stronger protections; violations carry civil money penalties of up to $10,000 per violation or $1,000,000 for repeated patterns.
If a doctor refers an enrollee to the emergency department, or plan authorizers do not respond within 30 minutes, follow-up care is deemed approved and cannot later be denied.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance plans and managed care companies, which would have to pay claims they currently deny, maintain 24-hour authorization lines, and face civil fines. Those costs would be passed on partly through premiums paid by employers and enrollees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and managed care plans

drawbacks.text: Requiring plans to pay for all emergency department visits regardless of network status or final diagnosis raises insurers' claims costs, which flow into premiums for employers and enrollees.

Higher emergency department reimbursement could encourage use of expensive emergency rooms for non-emergencies; the bill acknowledges this by allowing plans to impose a reasonable copayment to deter inappropriate use.

The bill is a broad federal mandate covering nearly every health plan, which some would object to as overreach into insurance regulation traditionally handled by states — though it explicitly preserves stronger state laws.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real but modest: paying fair claims for emergency care costs insurers money and ultimately premiums, against the harms the bill itself documents — patients stuck with bills for emergencies they prudently treated, and emergency departments threatening to close under unpaid burdens. The prudent-layperson standard and no-prior-authorization rule were later adopted as mainstream policy for Medicare and Medicaid managed care, suggesting the design was workable.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Sen. Barbara Mikulski introduced the Access to Emergency Medical Services Act of 1995 on September 12, 1995, drawing on findings that health plans routinely deny payment for federally required emergency services based on lack of prior approval or retroactive judgment that the condition was not an emergency.
Eleven senators cosponsored the bill, 10 Democrats and 1 Republican, giving it bipartisan support.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources on the day of introduction; that was the last action of any kind recorded for the bill.
The bill received no committee markup, no floor vote, and no further consideration before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Managed care and health insurance plans were better off: they could keep denying emergency claims for lack of prior approval or network status, and the cost of those denials stayed on patients and emergency departments.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health plans that deny emergency claims

for.name: Sen. Barbara Mikulski
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks citing federal law requiring emergency departments to treat everyone while plans refuse to pay.

for.name: 11 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan backing.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by a Republican in the 104th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a markup or any further action, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Managed care industry
against.role: Health plans and HMOs whose payment practices the bill targeted
against.what_they_did: The bill's own findings describe plans routinely denying payment for federally required emergency services; industry groups broadly opposed emergency-care coverage mandates during the 1990s managed-care patient-protection debates, which culminated only in 1997 with narrower requirements.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship (10 Democrats, 1 Republican) but no votes ever occurred, so the partisan shape of any opposition is not in the record.

industries.industry: Managed care plans and health insurers
industries.note: The bill would force them to pay for emergency care they currently deny, keep 24/7 authorization staff available, and expose them to fines up to $1 million for patterns of violations. Their gain from the status quo is the cost borne by sick patients and emergency departments.

industries.industry: Emergency physicians and hospital emergency departments
industries.note: Federal law requires them to evaluate and stabilize everyone regardless of insurance, so unpaid claims fall directly on them. The bill requires plans to pay a reasonable amount for that care, shoring up emergency departments' finances.

Mandated emergency coverage would raise claims costs that show up in premiums, but enrollees gain protection from surprise denials of emergency bills — the exact situation the bill's findings describe.
